summary:
Ranger is a web app that helps farmers decide what to plant, and in what order, using 25 years of free NASA Earth data. Farmers face hotter weather, less predictable rain, water shortages and tired soil, and NASA's data is hard for them to use. Ranger turns it into simple, explained answers for any field on Earth.

A farmer types a place or draws a field on the map. Ranger builds a land passport: salinity, drought and fire risk, the water balance, and the crops that fit. Its Rotation Planner compares the farmer's current rotation with three alternatives, scoring each from 0 to 100 on water, nitrogen, soil structure, erosion, pest-cycle break, income and animal feed. Sliders let farmers set their own priorities or test a hotter, drier future, and the ranking updates live. Each strategy explains why it was suggested, the NASA evidence behind it, its benefits, its gaps and risks. A bare-field calendar shows when the field sits empty and when heat, frost or water stress hits.

Ranger uses MODIS, NASA POWER, GPM and SRTM today, and SMAP, GRACE-FO and Landsat through Google Earth Engine. It works in English and Uzbek, and supports farmers and agronomists rather than replacing them.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Ranger is a web app that helps farmers decide what to plant, and in what order, using 25 years of free NASA Earth data. A farmer types a place or draws a field on the map (up to 100 km², anywhere on Earth). Ranger then pulls NASA data for that exact area and builds:

• Land passport: salinity, drought and fire risk scores (0–100), the water balance (rain vs. crop water demand), the best land use and the crops that fit.

• Rotation Planner: the farmer's current rotation next to three alternatives, each scored 0–100 on seven criteria: water use, nitrogen, soil structure, erosion control, pest-cycle break, income and animal feed. Priority sliders let farmers choose what matters most, and "what if" sliders test a drier or hotter future. The ranking updates live.

• Explanations: every strategy shows why it was suggested, the NASA evidence behind it, its benefits, and its gaps and risks that need local review.

• Bare-field calendar: month by month, when the field usually sits empty (MODIS NDVI) and when heat, frost or water stress hits (NASA POWER).

• An AI chat that explains the results in plain language, and a printable PDF report.

Scores come from transparent, rule-based models on NASA data, and 25-year trends are tested with Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope statistics. The AI only explains results; it does not invent numbers. A new field shows first results in about 14 seconds, while the full satellite history loads in the background.

What benefits does it have?

• Saves water: shows which rotations need less irrigation.

• Protects soil: suggests rotations with legumes that add nitrogen, break pest cycles and keep the soil covered.

• Easy to use: no coding, maps or science skills needed; English and Uzbek.

• Trustworthy: every plan shows its evidence and says what it does not know.

• Global: works for any field on Earth; demo farms in Uzbekistan, California, Punjab, the Nile Delta and Brazil.

What is the intended impact?

Farming uses about 70% of the fresh water people take, and the Aral Sea shows what happens when water is used without planning. Ranger helps farmers and agronomists make better crop choices before they plant, to save water, keep soil healthy and adapt to a changing climate. It also serves water managers, schools and universities (a real NASA data lab for students), researchers and governments (drought, salt and frost risk). Next steps: pilot farms in dry, tropical and temperate climates, ECOSTRESS, risk zones inside a field, and local prices and crops.

What tools did we use?

• NASA data: MODIS (NDVI, salt index, burned area, via ORNL DAAC), NASA POWER (heat, frost, evaporation, soil moisture), GPM IMERG (rainfall), SRTM (elevation and slope), FIRMS (fire). SMAP, GRACE-FO and Landsat are integrated through Google Earth Engine and switch on with a key; ECOSTRESS is next. NASA GIBS imagery for visuals.

• Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall, Shapely.

• Frontend: TypeScript, React, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet and Geoman (field drawing), ECharts (charts).

• AI: Claude (Anthropic) for the plain-language chat and explanations.

• No special hardware: it runs in any web browser, on desktop or phone.

How is it creative?

Most tools show raw maps or a single crop list. Ranger turns many NASA datasets into one simple decision, compares rotations side by side, and lets farmers re-rank them live by their own priorities and future climate. Every suggestion explains itself with NASA evidence, and the bare-field calendar shows the exact months a new crop can fill.

What factors did we consider?

• Farmers with little technical experience: plain words, simple scores, local language.

• Honesty: satellites cannot see which crop is planted, so the farmer enters their current rotation; data resolution and missing local prices are shown as gaps.

• Local expertise: Ranger supports, but does not replace, farmers and agronomists.

• Speed and reliability: caching and a two-step build so results appear quickly.

• Water, soil health, income and animal feed together, not just yield.
